query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper HEA nanoparticles, the onset of premelting and melting is governed by local compositional segregation that concentrates the lower-melting element (copper) at the nanoparticle surfaces, thereby reducing local cohesive bonding and initiating melting at lower temperatures than a chemically homogenized particle.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, equiatomic high-entropy alloy nanoparticles of Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu with a random solid solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: Modifying the synthesis or post-synthesis annealing treatment to either promote or suppress surface segregation of copper, for example by varying cooling rates to control atomic mobility.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted across the premelting to melting temperature regime under controlled inert or high-vacuum conditions to prevent oxidation; nanoparticle sizes held constant to isolate the effect of chemical ordering.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical short-range order (CSRO) fluctuations leading to copper enrichment at interfaces and surface facets, which weakens local metal–metal cohesive interactions.
generation.mechanism: Thermal energy during heating mobilizes atoms; due to differences in atomic size and bonding energies, copper atoms (which have a lower melting point and reduced cohesive energy relative to the other constituents) preferentially segregate toward the nanoparticle surface. This segregation creates localized regions with weakened bonding that act as nucleation sites for premelting, thereby governing the overall melting behavior of the nanoparticle.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles that exhibit pronounced surface premelting at temperatures below the bulk melting point, with the onset temperature being lower in particles that show higher surface copper segregation compared to those with a more homogeneous element distribution.
generation.baseline: A nanoparticle batch processed with rapid cooling to lock in a homogeneous distribution of elements, which should show higher overall premelting/melting temperatures and more uniform melting behavior.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies primarily to nanoparticles in the size regime where surface-to-volume effects are significant (typically below tens of nanometers) and for compositions with substantial differences in individual elemental melting points and cohesive energies. It may not apply if nanoparticle size or synthesis conditions dramatically alter atomic mobility or if the alloy composition is significantly shifted from equiatomic ratios.
generation.uncertainty: The precise degree of copper surface enrichment required to trigger the observed phenomena and the quantification of its effect on the melting onset temperature remain uncertain without further experimental calibration. In addition, the role of possible competing effects from other elements (e.g., chromium or cobalt) in modifying local bonding is not fully defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles: one set with rapid quenching to preserve a homogeneous elemental distribution, and a second set with controlled slow cooling to enhance atomic mobility and promote surface copper segregation. Characterize the surface chemical composition of both sets using techniques such as atom probe tomography or XPS. Then, subject both sets to incremental heating under identical atmospheres and monitor the onset of premelting using in situ TEM or differential scanning calorimetry.
measurements: Surface elemental distribution (especially copper concentration) via atom probe tomography or XPS
Onset temperature of surface premelting and full melting via in situ TEM imaging or DSC
Local structural changes monitored by high-resolution electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with enhanced surface copper segregation do not exhibit a statistically significant lower premelting or melting onset temperature relative to the homogeneous baseline, or if homogeneous nanoparticles also show similar early premelting behavior without evidence of copper enrichment, then the proposed mechanism of copper-driven surface premelting is refuted.

The more the better: on the formation of single-phase high entropy alloy nanoparticles as catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction†

Abstract: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are an important new material class with significant application potential in catalysis and electrocatalysis. The entropy-driven formation of HEA materials requires high temperatures and controlled cooling rates. However, catalysts in general also require highly dispersed materials, i.e., nanoparticles. Only then a favorable utilization of the expensive raw materials can be achieved. Several recently reported HEA nanoparticle synthesis strategies, therefore, avoid the high-temperature regime to prevent particle growth. In our work, we investigate a system of five noble metal single-source precursors with superior catalytic activity for the oxygen reduction reaction. Combining in situ X-ray powder diffraction with multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we address the fundamental question of how single-phase HEA nanoparticles can form at low temperatures. Periodicity in the Electrochemical Dissolution of Transition Metals

Abstract: AbstractExtensive research efforts are currently dedicated to the search for new electrocatalyst materials in which expensive and rare noble metals are replaced with cheaper and more abundant transition metals. Recently, numerous alloys, oxides, and composites with such metals have been identified as highly active electrocatalysts through the use of high‐throughput screening methods with the help of activity descriptors. Up to this point, stability has lacked such descriptors. Hence, we elucidate the role of intrinsic metal/oxide properties on the corrosion behavior of representative 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metals. Electrochemical dissolution of nine transition metals is quantified using online inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP‐MS). Based on the obtained dissolution data in alkaline and acidic media, we establish clear periodic correlations between the amount of dissolved metal, the cohesive energy of the metal atoms (E coh), and the energy of oxygen adsorption on the metal (ΔH O,ads). Such correlations can support the knowledge‐driven search for more stable electrocatalysts.Keywords: c
